Clustering, explained and benchmarked

e-means vs k-means, side by side

An illustrated tour of a new clustering optimizer from FAIR at Meta, and where it does and doesn't beat the classic.

k-means has been the default clustering algorithm for 40 years. In November 2026, Bessa et al. published e-means (arXiv 2611.09501), which claims to reach k-means' loss "in one-tenth the epochs." This notebook explains what e-means changes, builds it from scratch in about 30 lines of NumPy, then races it against Lloyd's k-means in seven situations chosen so that each method gets a chance to win, tie or fail.

Contents 1. The problem both methods solve 2. How Lloyd's k-means works 3. How e-means works (and a from-scratch version) 4. Watching them move 5. Seven head-to-head scenarios 6. Scorecard and takeaways

Runs on a laptop CPU in about 5 to 10 minutes. Needs faiss-cpu>=1.16, scikit-learn, matplotlib, pandas, scipy. Fashion-MNIST (about 30 MB) is downloaded on first run.

e-meansLloyd k-meansMini-batch k-means

Shared helpers

Timing excludes scoring. Every method starts from the same random rows for a given seed, so differences come from the algorithm, not the luck of the start.

Code 74 lines
def init_rows(x, k, seed=0):
    return np.ascontiguousarray(x[np.sort(np.random.default_rng(seed).choice(len(x), k, replace=False))])

def mse(x, c):
    D, _ = faiss.knn(np.ascontiguousarray(x, dtype="float32"), np.ascontiguousarray(c, dtype="float32"), 1)
    return float(D.mean())

def assign(x, c):
    _, I = faiss.knn(np.ascontiguousarray(x, dtype="float32"), np.ascontiguousarray(c, dtype="float32"), 1)
    return I.ravel()

def lloyd(x, k, iters=25, seed=0, x_test=None, keep=(), start=None):
    """Faiss Lloyd k-means, one iteration at a time so each one can be scored
    (same result as a single multi-iteration run). Returns per-iteration records."""
    c, t_total, recs, snaps = (init_rows(x, k, seed) if start is None else start), 0.0, [], {}
    for it in range(1, iters + 1):
        km = faiss.Kmeans(x.shape[1], k, niter=1, seed=seed + it, max_points_per_centroid=10**9,
                          min_points_per_centroid=1)
        t = time.perf_counter(); km.train(x, init_centroids=c); t_total += time.perf_counter() - t
        c = km.centroids.copy()
        recs.append(dict(method="Lloyd k-means", epochs=it, time=t_total, train_mse=mse(x, c),
                         test_mse=mse(x_test, c) if x_test is not None else np.nan))
        if it in keep: snaps[it] = c
    return pd.DataFrame(recs), c, snaps

def emeans(x, k, epochs=2, seed=0, start=None):
    em = NumpyEmeans(x.shape[1], k, nepochs=epochs, seed=seed)
    start = init_rows(x, k, seed) if start is None else start
    t = time.perf_counter(); c, lab = em.train(x, init_centroids=start); t = time.perf_counter() - t
    return np.ascontiguousarray(c, dtype="float32"), t, em

def emeans_curve(x, k, epochs=(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5), seed=0, x_test=None, start=None):
    """Each budget is its own run, because e-means' step schedule depends on the budget."""
    recs, c = [], None
    for T in epochs:
        c, t, _ = emeans(x, k, T, seed, start)
        recs.append(dict(method="e-means", epochs=T, time=t, train_mse=mse(x, c),
                         test_mse=mse(x_test, c) if x_test is not None else np.nan))
    return pd.DataFrame(recs), c

def race(x, k, seed=0, x_test=None, iters=25, epochs=(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5), start=None):
    a, cl, _ = lloyd(x, k, iters, seed, x_test, start=start)
    b, ce = emeans_curve(x, k, epochs, seed, x_test, start)
    return pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True), cl, ce

def match(df, col="train_mse"):
    """Lloyd's final loss, and the first e-means budget that reaches it (if any)."""
    ref = df[df.method == "Lloyd k-means"].iloc[-1]
    em = df[df.method == "e-means"].sort_values("epochs")
    hit = em[em[col] <= ref[col]]
    best = em[col].min()
    out = dict(lloyd_loss=ref[col], lloyd_time=ref.time, emeans_best_loss=best,
               loss_change_pct=100 * (best / ref[col] - 1))
    if len(hit):
        out.update(epochs_to_match=hit.epochs.iloc[0], time_to_match=hit.time.iloc[0],
                   speedup=ref.time / hit.time.iloc[0])
    else:
        out.update(epochs_to_match=np.nan, time_to_match=np.nan, speedup=np.nan)
    return out

def plot_race(df, ax, title, col="train_mse", xcol="time"):
    ref = df[df.method == "Lloyd k-means"][col].iloc[-1]
    for m, g in df.groupby("method"):
        g = g.sort_values(xcol)
        y = 100 * (g[col] / ref - 1)
        ax.plot(g[xcol], y, "-o", color=COLORS[m], lw=2, ms=3.5, label=m)
        above = m == "Lloyd k-means"          # Lloyd's label above its line end, e-means' below
        ax.annotate(m, (g[xcol].iloc[-1], y.iloc[-1]), xytext=(-4, 12 if above else -13), textcoords="offset points",
                    ha="right", fontsize=8.5, color=COLORS[m], fontweight="bold")
    ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=1, ls="--")
    ax.set_xscale("log"); ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(PLAIN); ax.xaxis.set_minor_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: ""))
    ax.set_title(title)
    ax.set_xlabel("training time, seconds (log)" if xcol == "time" else "passes over the data (log)")
    ax.set_ylabel({"train_mse": "train MSE", "test_mse": "test MSE"}[col] + " vs Lloyd's final, %")

1. The problem both methods solve

Given \(n\) points and a number \(k\), find \(k\) centroids \(c_1,\dots,c_k\) that minimize the mean squared distance from each point to its nearest centroid:

\[\text{MSE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \min_j \lVert x_i - c_j \rVert^2\]

Both methods minimize exactly this objective. e-means is not a new kind of cluster. It is a faster, better-behaved way to search for the same answer. That single fact predicts most of what follows: e-means should win on time and final loss, and should be no help at all when k-means is the wrong model for the data.

2. Lloyd's k-means

The 1957/1982 algorithm everyone learns:

  1. Pick \(k\) starting centroids (random points, or k-means++).
  2. Assign every point to its nearest centroid. (one full pass over all \(n\) points)
  3. Update every centroid to the mean of its points.
  4. Repeat 2 to 3 until nothing changes, or for a fixed number of iterations (Faiss defaults to 25).

Each iteration is guaranteed not to increase the loss, but every centroid moves only once per full pass over the data. With millions of points and thousands of clusters, that is slow, and centroids that start in empty regions can end up with no points at all ("dead clusters").

3. How e-means works

e-means updates centroids from small random batches instead of full passes, so each centroid moves hundreds of times per pass. Mini-batch k-means did that in 2010, but it usually stalls at a worse loss and needs hand-tuning. e-means adds five ingredients:

Ingredient What it does Why it helps
EMA statistics each cluster keeps a running count \(N_j\) and sum \(S_j\); the centroid is \(c_j = S_j / N_j\) old batches fade out smoothly instead of being averaged forever
Cosine step schedule the step \(\alpha = 1-\gamma\) starts at \(\alpha_0\) and decays to \(0.1\,\alpha_0\) big moves early, fine-tuning late
Dead-cluster revival every 5 batches, a cluster with under 10% of the average count is re-born by splitting a busy one no wasted centroids (the paper's biggest single gain)
Last-epoch mean at the end, each centroid becomes the plain mean of the points it got in the final pass a cheap final polish that is guaranteed to lower training loss
Scaling laws batch size \(B\) and \(\alpha_0\) come from formulas in \(n\), \(k\) and the epoch budget \(T\) nothing to tune

The update for each batch, where \(n_j\) and \(s_j\) are the batch's count and sum for cluster \(j\):

\[N_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,N_j + \alpha\, n_j \qquad S_j \leftarrow (1-\alpha)\,S_j + \alpha\, s_j \qquad c_j = S_j / N_j\]

The scaling laws, and what they pick

From the Faiss e-means README. The batch size is rounded to a power of two and capped at about n/2; the step is clamped to [0.0001, 1].

Code 16 lines
def recipe(n, k, T, d):
    """e-means' scaling laws: batch size and starting step from (n, k, epochs)."""
    c = 0.00439175 if d <= 16 else 0.035134          # 'quality' batch at low dimension, 'throughput' otherwise
    B = c * k**0.134749 * n**0.876473 * T**0.813344
    B = int(min(2 ** round(math.log2(max(B, 1))), n // 2))
    a0 = float(np.clip(0.8244 * k**-0.4617 * B**0.9003 * n**-0.4498 * T**-0.1057, 1e-4, 1.0))
    return B, a0

rows = []
for n, k, d in [(20_000, 15, 2), (60_000, 256, 64), (60_000, 2048, 64), (1_000_000, 4096, 1536), (100_000_000, 262_144, 96)]:
    B, a0 = recipe(n, k, 2, d)
    lib = NumpyEmeans(d, k, nepochs=2); lib.begin(n, np.zeros((k, d), "float32")) if n * d <= 2e8 else None
    rows.append(dict(n=f"{n:,}", k=f"{k:,}", d=d, batch=B, alpha0=round(a0, 4),
                     library_batch=lib.recipe["batch_size"] if lib.recipe else "-",
                     updates_per_pass=math.ceil(n / B)))

e-means from scratch

The whole algorithm in plain NumPy, following the paper's Algorithm 1. The Faiss version is the same idea with fast kernels and a few refinements (it picks the donor cluster more carefully, for example).

Code 54 lines
def emeans_scratch(x, k, epochs=2, seed=0, revive_every=5, tau=0.1, floor=0.1, donor="mass"):
    n, d = x.shape
    B, a0 = recipe(n, k, epochs, d)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    c0 = init_rows(x, k, seed).astype(np.float64)
    N = np.full(k, 1e-10)                       # tiny weight: the start is forgotten after one batch
    S = c0 * N[:, None]
    steps = math.ceil(n / B); M = epochs * steps; t = 0
    for ep in range(epochs):
        order = rng.permutation(n)
        last = ep == epochs - 1
        if last:
            tot_s, tot_n = np.zeros((k, d)), np.zeros(k)
        for i in range(0, n, B):
            xb = x[order[i:i + B]]
            a = assign(xb, S / N[:, None])                                   # nearest centroid
            onehot = sparse.csr_matrix((np.ones(len(a)), (a, np.arange(len(a)))), shape=(k, len(a)))
            n_j, s_j = np.asarray(onehot.sum(1)).ravel(), onehot @ xb        # batch counts and sums
            alpha = a0 * (floor + (1 - floor) * 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * t / M)))   # cosine schedule
            N = (1 - alpha) * N + alpha * n_j                                # EMA update
            S = (1 - alpha) * S + alpha * s_j
            if last:
                tot_s += s_j; tot_n += n_j
            t += 1
            if t % revive_every == 0:                                        # dead-cluster revival
                dead, alive = np.where(N < tau * N.mean())[0], np.where(N >= tau * N.mean())[0]
                m = min(len(dead), len(alive))
                if m:
                    if donor == "mass":      # the paper: donors drawn at random, in proportion to their mass
                        src = rng.choice(alive, m, replace=False, p=N[alive] / N[alive].sum())
                    else:                    # variant: always split the heaviest clusters
                        src = alive[np.argsort(N[alive])[::-1][:m]]
                    for j, s in zip(dead[:m], src):
                        cs = S[s] / N[s]
                        nudge = 1e-4 * np.abs(cs).mean() * rng.standard_normal(d)
                        N[j] = N[s] = N[s] / 2                               # split the donor's mass in two
                        S[j], S[s] = (cs + nudge) * N[j], (cs - nudge) * N[s]
    c = S / N[:, None]
    seen = tot_n > 0
    c[seen] = tot_s[seen] / tot_n[seen, None]                                # last-epoch mean
    return c.astype("float32")

An experiment: which cluster should donate?

When e-means revives a dead centroid, it splits a donor cluster picked at random in proportion to its mass. Here the true answer has 200 blobs and the random start doubles up centroids in many of them, so splitting the heaviest clusters instead (they're the ones likely holding two blobs) might help. It's a one-line change:

Code 9 lines
rows = []
for seed in range(3):
    a = emeans_scratch(x_demo, k, 2, seed)
    b = emeans_scratch(x_demo, k, 2, seed, donor="largest")
    rows.append(dict(seed=seed, paper_donor_rule=mse(x_demo, a), split_heaviest=mse(x_demo, b),
                     lloyd_25_iterations=lloyd(x_demo, k, 25, seed)[0].train_mse.iloc[-1]))
r = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("seed"); r.loc["mean"] = r.mean()
print(f"Optimal loss for this data is about {16 * 1.5**2:.0f} (16 dims x noise variance 1.5^2).")

On this data the greedy rule gets much closer to the optimum. That doesn't make it better in general: the paper's random rule is designed to be robust across very different datasets, and we've tested one. But it shows how much of e-means' advantage comes from revival, and how easy the algorithm is to experiment with.

4. Watching them move

20 well-separated blobs in 2D, both methods started from the same 20 random points. Lines trace each centroid's path from its start (hollow) to its end (filled). Lloyd takes a few big jumps, one per full pass. e-means takes hundreds of small steps within a single pass, and its revival step teleports stranded centroids to where they're needed.

Code 35 lines
x2, y2 = make_blobs(30_000, centers=20, cluster_std=0.9, center_box=(-25, 25), random_state=7)
x2 = x2.astype("float32"); k2 = 20
start = init_rows(x2, k2, seed=3)

# Lloyd path: centroids after each iteration
path_l, c = [start], start
for it in range(25):
    km = faiss.Kmeans(2, k2, niter=1, seed=it, max_points_per_centroid=10**9, min_points_per_centroid=1)
    km.train(x2, init_centroids=c); c = km.centroids.copy(); path_l.append(c)

# e-means path: centroids after every batch, using the library's step-by-step API.
# (At d <= 2 the library turns revival off by default; we turn it on here to show it.)
em = NumpyEmeans(2, k2, nepochs=1, seed=3, unused_threshold=0.1)
em.begin(len(x2), start)
rng, B, path_e = np.random.default_rng(3), em.recipe["batch_size"], [start]
for rows in em.recipe["epoch_rows"]:
    order = rng.permutation(len(x2))[:rows]
    for i in range(0, rows, B):
        em.update(em.accumulate(x2[order[i:i + B]]))
        path_e.append(np.array(em.current_centroids()))
    em.end_epoch()
c_e = np.asarray(em.finalize()); path_e.append(c_e)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 5.2), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, path, name, sub in [(axes[0], path_l, "Lloyd k-means", "25 full passes"),
                            (axes[1], path_e, "e-means", f"1 pass, {len(path_e) - 2} small updates")]:
    P = np.stack(path)
    ax.scatter(x2[::6, 0], x2[::6, 1], s=1, color="#c3c2b7", rasterized=True)
    for j in range(k2):
        ax.plot(P[:, j, 0], P[:, j, 1], color=COLORS[name], lw=1, alpha=0.8)
    ax.scatter(P[0, :, 0], P[0, :, 1], s=30, facecolors="white", edgecolors=COLORS[name], lw=1.5, zorder=3)
    ax.scatter(P[-1, :, 0], P[-1, :, 1], s=36, color=COLORS[name], edgecolors="white", lw=1, zorder=4)
    ax.set_title(f"{name}: {sub}\nfinal MSE {mse(x2, P[-1]):.2f}, ARI vs true blobs {ARI(y2, assign(x2, P[-1])):.2f}")
    ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout()

Same start, same data. Neither method fixes every bad start: both still have some blobs sharing two centroids. But e-means got to a lower loss within its first pass, and you can see revival at work in the long blue jump, where a stranded centroid was re-born next to a busy cluster and then walked to its own blob.

5. Seven head-to-head scenarios

# Situation Prediction from section 1
A Few, well-separated clusters tie: both find the answer quickly
B Many clusters in high dimensions e-means wins on time
C Same data, growing k e-means' lead grows with k
D Real images with labels (Fashion-MNIST) lower loss, but not better label agreement
E Very uneven cluster sizes e-means avoids wasted clusters; mini-batch k-means is a real rival
F Clusters that aren't round blobs both fail the same way
G Low-dimensional data: photo color palette lower loss, smaller speed gain

A. Few, well-separated clusters

10 blobs in 10 dimensions, k = 10: the easy case k-means was designed for. Here both methods start from k-means++ seeds (spread-out starting points, the usual choice for small k), so neither begins with two centroids in one blob.

4 4 1.0 1.0 9.9858 9.9858 0.0839

With a sensible start both recover the blobs and reach the same loss. Everything finishes in a fraction of a second, so there is little for e-means to speed up. (With purely random starts, both get stuck with two centroids in one blob on most seeds; e-means' revival doesn't help there, because a shared blob still gives each centroid plenty of points.)

B. Many clusters in high dimensions

A 64-dimensional mixture of 1,024 overlapping Gaussian clusters, 200,000 points, k = 1,024. This is closer to what e-means was built for: embeddings, many centroids, lots of data. Test loss is on 20,000 held-out points.

Code 16 lines
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
centers = rng.normal(0, 1, (1024, 64))
yb = rng.integers(0, 1024, 220_000)
xb_all = (centers[yb] + 0.6 * rng.normal(size=(220_000, 64))).astype("float32")
xb, xb_test = xb_all[:200_000], xb_all[200_000:]
dfb, clb, ceb = race(xb, 1024, 0, x_test=xb_test)
mb = match(dfb, "test_mse")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
plot_race(dfb, axes[0], "B. Test loss vs time (n=200k, d=64, k=1,024)", col="test_mse")
plot_race(dfb, axes[1], "B. Test loss vs passes over the data", col="test_mse", xcol="epochs")
plt.tight_layout()
print(f"Lloyd, 25 iterations: test MSE {mb['lloyd_loss']:.4f} in {mb['lloyd_time']:.1f}s")
print(f"e-means matched it after {mb['epochs_to_match']} epochs in {mb['time_to_match']:.1f}s ({mb['speedup']:.1f}x faster); "
      f"best e-means test MSE {mb['emeans_best_loss']:.4f} ({mb['loss_change_pct']:+.2f}%)")
SCORE.append(dict(scenario="B. Many clusters, high-dimensional", winner="e-means",
                  evidence=f"matched Lloyd's 25-iteration test loss {mb['speedup']:.1f}x faster; {mb['loss_change_pct']:+.2f}% loss at 5 epochs"))

Lloyd, 25 iterations: test MSE 29.2828 in 9.3s

C. Where the advantage grows: sweeping k

Fashion-MNIST (60,000 clothing images, projected to 64 dimensions with PCA), same data, k from 16 to 2,048. For each k: how much faster e-means reaches Lloyd's 25-iteration loss. Median of 3 seeds.

Code 19 lines
def fashion_mnist(cache="fashion_mnist"):
    base = "https://storage.googleapis.com/tensorflow/tf-keras-datasets/"
    os.makedirs(cache, exist_ok=True)
    out = {}
    for name, off in [("train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", 16), ("train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz", 8),
                      ("t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz", 16), ("t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz", 8)]:
        p = os.path.join(cache, name)
        if not os.path.exists(p):
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + name, p)
        with gzip.open(p) as f:
            out[name] = np.frombuffer(f.read(), np.uint8, offset=off)
    xtr = out["train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz"].reshape(-1, 784).astype("float32") / 255
    xte = out["t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz"].reshape(-1, 784).astype("float32") / 255
    return xtr, out["train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz"], xte, out["t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz"]

fm_x, fm_y, fm_xt, fm_yt = fashion_mnist()
pca = PCA(64, random_state=0).fit(fm_x)
fm64, fm64_t = pca.transform(fm_x).astype("float32"), pca.transform(fm_xt).astype("float32")
print(fm64.shape, f"PCA keeps {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.0%} of the variance")

(60000, 64) PCA keeps 88% of the variance
Code 27 lines
rows = []
for k in [16, 64, 256, 1024, 2048]:
    for seed in range(3):
        df, _, _ = race(fm64, k, seed, epochs=(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 5))
        rows.append(dict(k=k, seed=seed, **match(df)))
rc = pd.DataFrame(rows).groupby("k").median(numeric_only=True).drop(columns="seed")
display(rc[["lloyd_time", "epochs_to_match", "time_to_match", "speedup", "loss_change_pct"]])

ax = axes[0]

for k_, s in rc.speedup.items():
    ax.annotate(f"{s:.1f}x", (k_, s), xytext=(0, 7), textcoords="offset points", ha="center", fontsize=8, color=INK)
ax.axhline(1, color=MUTED, lw=1, ls="--")
ax.set_xscale("log", base=2); ax.set_ylim(0, rc.speedup.max() * 1.25)
ax.set_xticks(rc.index, [f"{k_:,}" for k_ in rc.index]); ax.minorticks_off()
ax.set(title="C. e-means speedup to reach Lloyd's 25-iteration loss", xlabel="number of clusters k (log)", ylabel="speedup (x)")
ax = axes[1]
bars = ax.bar(range(len(rc)), rc.loss_change_pct, color=COLORS["e-means"], width=0.6)
ax.bar_label(bars, [f"{v:.1f}%" for v in rc.loss_change_pct], padding=3, fontsize=8, color=INK)

ax.axhline(0, color=MUTED, lw=1)

This is the paper's central claim in miniature: the more clusters you ask for, the more full passes Lloyd needs, and the bigger e-means' head start.

D. Real images with labels: does lower loss mean better clusters?

Fashion-MNIST with k = 10, compared against the 10 true clothing categories. The centroids are shown as images (mapped back from PCA space).

A lower k-means loss is not the same as matching human categories: sandals, sneakers and ankle boots are close in pixel space no matter how well you optimize. If label agreement is the goal, the fix is a better representation or a different model, not a better optimizer.

E. Very uneven cluster sizes

1,000 true clusters in 32 dimensions whose sizes follow a power law (a few huge, most tiny), k = 1,000. Random starts put most centroids in the big clusters, so the question is who rescues the rest. scikit-learn's mini-batch k-means joins this race because it has its own small-cluster reassignment.

Code 32 lines
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
K, d = 1000, 32
cent = rng.normal(0, 4, (K, d))
w = 1 / np.arange(1, K + 1) ** 1.1; w /= w.sum()
ye = rng.choice(K, 220_000, p=w)
xe_all = (cent[ye] + rng.normal(size=(220_000, d))).astype("float32")
xe, xe_t, ye_tr = xe_all[:200_000], xe_all[200_000:], ye[:200_000]

dfe, cle, cee = race(xe, K, 0, x_test=xe_t)
mbk = MiniBatchKMeans(K, init=init_rows(xe, K, 0), n_init=1, batch_size=4096, random_state=0, max_iter=5,
                      max_no_improvement=None, tol=0)
t0 = time.perf_counter(); mbk.fit(xe); t_mbk = time.perf_counter() - t0
cm = mbk.cluster_centers_.astype("float32")

res = []
for name, c, t in [("Lloyd k-means", cle, dfe[dfe.method == "Lloyd k-means"].time.iloc[-1]),
                   ("e-means", cee, dfe[dfe.method == "e-means"].time.iloc[-1]),
                   ("Mini-batch k-means", cm, t_mbk)]:
    sizes = np.bincount(assign(xe, c), minlength=K)
    res.append(dict(method=name, seconds=t, test_mse=mse(xe_t, c), true_clusters_covered=len(np.unique(assign(c, cent.astype("float32")))),
                    near_empty=(sizes < 0.1 * len(xe) / K).sum(), _sizes=np.sort(sizes)[::-1]))
re_ = pd.DataFrame(res)
display(re_.drop(columns="_sizes"))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
for _, r in re_.iterrows():
    ax.plot(np.arange(1, K + 1), np.maximum(r._sizes, 0.8), color=COLORS[r.method], lw=2, label=r.method)
ax.set_yscale("log"); ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(PLAIN)
ax.set(title="E. Cluster sizes, largest to smallest", xlabel="cluster rank", ylabel="points (log)")
ax.legend(); plt.tight_layout()
best = re_.loc[re_.test_mse.idxmin(), "method"]
SCORE.append(dict(scenario="E. Very uneven sizes", winner=f"{best} (lowest loss)",
                  evidence="; ".join(f"{r.method} {r.test_mse:.1f}" for _, r in re_.iterrows()) + " test MSE"))
method seconds test_mse true_clusters_covered near_empty
0 Lloyd k-means 1.5339 58.9587 473 18
1 e-means 0.7505 58.8389 447 0
2 Mini-batch k-means 1.7346 57.1525 518 15

true_clusters_covered counts how many of the 1,000 true clusters have at least one centroid closer to them than to any other true center; near_empty counts centroids with under 10% of an average cluster's points.

This is the hardest case for every method, and an honest one to include. e-means leaves no near-empty clusters and edges out Lloyd on loss in less time, but scikit-learn's mini-batch k-means, which reassigns small clusters aggressively, reaches the lowest loss and covers the most true clusters. e-means' revival splits heavy clusters, so it tends to put extra centroids into the biggest true clusters rather than finding the tiny ones.

F. Clusters that aren't round

Two moons, two rings and stretched blobs. k-means (of any kind) cuts space into straight-edged cells around centroids, so it can't follow these shapes. Spectral clustering, a different model, is shown for contrast.

Code 20 lines
sets = {
    "Two moons": make_moons(1500, noise=0.06, random_state=0),
    "Two rings": make_circles(1500, noise=0.05, factor=0.45, random_state=0),
}
xs, ys = make_blobs(1500, centers=3, random_state=170)
sets["Stretched blobs"] = (xs @ np.array([[0.6, -0.64], [-0.41, 0.85]]), ys)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(10, 9.5))
pal = ["#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a"]
for r, (title, (x, y)) in enumerate(sets.items()):
    x = x.astype("float32"); kk = len(np.unique(y))
    _, cl, _ = lloyd(x, kk, 25, seed=0)
    ce, _, _ = emeans(x, kk, 5, seed=0)
    sc = SpectralClustering(kk, affinity="nearest_neighbors", n_neighbors=12, random_state=0).fit_predict(x)
    for col, (name, lab) in enumerate([("Lloyd k-means", assign(x, cl)), ("e-means", assign(x, ce)), ("Spectral", sc)]):
        ax = axes[r, col]
        ax.scatter(x[:, 0], x[:, 1], s=4, c=[pal[i % 3] for i in lab])
        ax.set_title(f"{title}: {name}\nARI {ARI(y, lab):.2f}", color=INK); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
plt.tight_layout()
SCORE.append(dict(scenario="F. Non-round clusters", winner="Neither (use another model)",
                  evidence="Lloyd and e-means draw the same straight-line splits; spectral clustering follows the shapes"))

Identical failures. A faster optimizer can't fix the wrong model. This is the clearest way to see that e-means is an optimizer improvement, not a new kind of clustering.

G. Low-dimensional data: choosing a photo's color palette

Color quantization is a classic k-means job: treat every pixel as a point in 3D color space and pick k = 16 colors. Each image below is redrawn using only its method's 16 colors.

Code 22 lines
img = load_sample_image("china.jpg")
px = (img.reshape(-1, 3) / 255).astype("float32")
k = 16
dfg, clg, ceg = race(px, k, 0, epochs=(0.5, 1, 2, 5))
_, _, snaps = lloyd(px, k, 2, 0, keep=(2,))
ce1, t1, _ = emeans(px, k, 1, 0)

def redraw(c): return c[assign(px, c)].reshape(img.shape)
panels = [("Original", None, None),
          ("Lloyd, 2 iterations", snaps[2], dfg[(dfg.method == "Lloyd k-means") & (dfg.epochs == 2)].time.iloc[0]),
          ("e-means, 1 epoch", ce1, t1),
          ("Lloyd, 25 iterations", clg, dfg[dfg.method == "Lloyd k-means"].time.iloc[-1]),
          ("e-means, 5 epochs", ceg, dfg[dfg.method == "e-means"].time.iloc[-1])]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(17, 3.6))
for ax, (title, c, t) in zip(axes, panels):
    ax.imshow(img if c is None else redraw(c)); ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); ax.grid(False)
    ax.set_title(title if c is None else f"{title}\nMSE {mse(px, c) * 1e3:.2f}e-3, {t:.2f}s", color=INK)
plt.tight_layout()
mg = match(dfg)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.4)); plot_race(dfg, ax, "G. Color palette (3D pixels, k=16)"); plt.tight_layout()
SCORE.append(dict(scenario="G. Low-dimensional (photo colors)", winner="e-means on loss, small time gain",
                  evidence=f"{mg['loss_change_pct']:+.1f}% loss vs Lloyd's 25 iterations; speedup to match {mg['speedup']:.1f}x"))

e-means' single pass already matches Lloyd's 25 iterations, visually and in loss. In 3 dimensions each Lloyd pass is cheap, though, so the wall-clock gain is modest, and the paper notes its scaling laws were tuned for high-dimensional embeddings.

Takeaways

  • Same objective, better optimizer. e-means minimizes exactly what k-means minimizes. It wins on time to a given loss and usually ends a little lower.
  • The win grows with scale. More clusters, more data and higher dimensions mean more full passes for Lloyd, and a bigger head start for e-means. In this notebook, on a laptop CPU, that ranged from about 2x to 20x (timings vary a little run to run); the paper reports 10 to 45x on GPUs with millions of points.
  • It does not fix the model. Non-round clusters, density differences and "do these match human labels?" are unchanged. Pick a different model (or better features) for those.
  • Small, low-dimensional problems are already fast with Lloyd. e-means still finds a lower loss there, but the speedup is modest.
  • Uneven cluster sizes are hard for everyone. e-means avoids empty clusters and beats Lloyd, but mini-batch k-means did better here.
  • Revival matters a lot. Changing which cluster donates in the from-scratch version moved the loss by about 30% on one dataset, which makes e-means a fun algorithm to experiment with.

Next: the companion notebook e_means_vs_kmeans.ipynb runs the large-scale version of scenario B on 1M real OpenAI text embeddings, including how the centroids perform as a vector-search index.

Paper: Bessa, Mazaré, Szilvasy, Touvron, Picard, Douze, Jégou. "e-means: outperforming k-means (in one-tenth the epochs)." arXiv 2611.09501, 2026. Code: faiss.contrib.e_means.
